title: Evil Intended, Good Intended: The End of Genesis
summary: Joseph mourns his father, has him embalmed, and leads a great procession of Egyptians and Israelites to bury him in the cave of Machpelah in Canaan. Afterward his brothers, afraid he will now take revenge, send a message asking forgiveness, and Joseph answers that what they intended for evil God intended for good. Joseph lives to 110, and before he dies he makes his brothers swear to carry his bones up to the promised land when God comes to their aid.
story: Genesis ends where much of its drama has been heading: with the family of promise alive, reconciled, and waiting. Jacob's burial in Canaan keeps the oath Joseph swore in Genesis 47 and plants the family's hope in the land God promised. The brothers' fear after Jacob's death shows that reconciliation begun in Genesis 45 still needed a final word, and Joseph gives it in one of the Bible's great summaries of providence. The book that began with God creating the heavens and the earth ends with a coffin in Egypt. But it ends on a promise: “God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land.” The book of Exodus opens with that promise under threat, as a new Pharaoh rises who does not know Joseph, and shows how God keeps it.
historical:
Jacob's body is embalmed in the Egyptian manner, the only time the Bible describes the practice for an Israelite apart from Joseph himself (v. 26). Genesis gives forty days for the embalming and seventy days of Egyptian mourning (v. 3). Egyptian practice varied, but the preparation of a body for burial could take about seventy days, so the figures fit the world they describe. The seventy days of public mourning mark the great honor Egypt paid to Joseph's father.

Joseph's age at death, 110 years, was regarded in Egyptian texts as the ideal length of a life, the lifespan claimed by wise men and great officials. The same age is given for Joshua (Joshua 24:29). The funeral procession, with Pharaoh's officials, the elders of Egypt, chariots, and horsemen, was a state funeral. Its route to the threshing floor of Atad, “across the Jordan” (v. 10), is puzzling, since the direct road from Egypt to Hebron did not cross the Jordan. Some think the phrase describes the site from a particular vantage point, and others that the procession took a longer route around the Dead Sea; its exact location is unknown.
cultural:
The chapter is full of the customs of death and mourning. Joseph falls on his father's face and kisses him. Mourning was public and loud, and professional or communal lamentation could last for days; Joseph adds a seven-day mourning in Canaan to the seventy days in Egypt. The Canaanites name the place Abel-mizraim, which sounds like the Hebrew for mourning of Egypt, while also meaning meadow of Egypt. Burial with one's ancestors in family land was a matter of deep importance, and the cave of Machpelah, bought by Abraham from Ephron the Hittite (Genesis 23), was the family's only legal foothold in Canaan.

The brothers' fear reflects a common assumption in a family world: a father's presence restrained old grudges, and his death could release them. Their offer to be Joseph's slaves (v. 18) is a last fulfillment of the dreams of Genesis 37 and a measure of how little they still trusted his forgiveness. Joseph's coffin, placed in Egypt rather than buried, would travel with Israel through the exodus (Exodus 13:19) to Shechem (Joshua 24:32).
literary: The chapter has three parts: Jacob's burial (vv. 1-14), the brothers' plea and Joseph's reply (vv. 15-21), and Joseph's last years and death (vv. 22-26). Its center is verse 20, where the whole Joseph story is gathered into one sentence built on two intentions and two opposites: “what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this.” Joseph's question, “Am I in the place of God?”, repeats almost exactly what Jacob once said to Rachel (30:2), though with a very different spirit. The book's final paragraph turns on a repeated phrase. Twice Joseph says that God will surely visit or attend to them (vv. 24-25), a Hebrew idiom that doubles the verb for emphasis. The same promise returns when God tells Moses at the burning bush that he has surely attended to his people (Exodus 3:16), and when Moses takes Joseph's bones out of Egypt (Exodus 13:19). Genesis ends not with a resolution but with a coffin and a promise, leaving the reader waiting with Israel.

outline.t: Joseph mourns and embalms his father
The procession to Canaan and Jacob's burial
The brothers' fear and Joseph's forgiveness
Joseph's last years, his charge, and his death

doctrines.note: Verse 20 is the Bible's classic statement of providence. Human beings act with real intentions, sometimes evil ones, and remain responsible for them; God acts in and through the same events with his own intention, which is good and which prevails. Joseph does not say that the brothers' evil was good, only that God used it to preserve many lives.

“Am I in the place of God?” Joseph refuses to take revenge because judgment belongs to God, not to him. Paul makes the same point when he tells believers to leave room for God's wrath rather than avenging themselves (Romans 12:19). Letting go of vengeance is not pretending no wrong was done; it is trusting the right judge.

Joseph, the most powerful man in Egypt, asks that his bones be carried to Canaan. His last words look past his own death to a promise God has sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Hebrews 11:22 counts this as faith: at the end of his life Joseph spoke about the exodus and gave instructions about his bones.

words.note: Chashav, to think, plan, or intend. Used twice in verse 20: the brothers intended evil, and God intended good. The word describes deliberate planning, not accident. The same act had two authors with opposite purposes, and the chapter insists that God's purpose, not theirs, determined its outcome.

Paqad, to visit, attend to, or take note of, often in the sense of intervening to act. Joseph uses it twice, doubled for emphasis each time (vv. 24-25): God will surely visit you. The same doubled verb appears in Exodus 3:16 and 13:19, making it the thread that ties the end of Genesis to the beginning of Israel's rescue.

Aron, a chest or box. Here it is Joseph's coffin (v. 26), its only use for a coffin in the Bible; elsewhere it names a chest for temple offerings and, most often, the ark of the covenant. Genesis ends with a box holding the bones of the man who saved his family, waiting to be carried home.

christ: Joseph's words in verse 20 are the Old Testament's clearest anticipation of how the church came to understand the cross. The apostles prayed that Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, “carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen” (Acts 4:28). As with Joseph, the evil was real and the guilty were responsible, and God intended the same event for good, to save many lives. Joseph's forgiveness of brothers who could hardly believe it also resembles the gospel's offer to people who fear judgment, and his refusal to take God's place points to the one who does sit in God's place and uses that authority to forgive. Hebrews 11:22 remembers Joseph for his hope in the exodus, the pattern of the greater rescue the New Testament finds in Christ. These are connections of theme and pattern; Genesis 50 itself speaks of God's providence, not of the Messiah.

hard.q: Did Jacob really leave a message asking Joseph to forgive his brothers, or did the brothers invent it?
hard.a:
Genesis records no such instruction from Jacob. His last words to his sons in chapter 49 say nothing about it, and he had never been told, as far as the narrative shows, that the brothers sold Joseph. Many readers therefore think the brothers invented or at least embellished the message out of fear, which would show how deeply they still doubted Joseph's forgiveness seventeen years after he first gave it (45:5; 47:28). Others point out that Genesis does not record every private conversation and that Jacob may well have said something like this. The text leaves the question open.

What the narrator does show is Joseph's response. He weeps when the message comes, perhaps because he sees that his brothers still do not trust him. He does not question them or test the claim. He answers their fear directly, twice telling them not to be afraid, and he promises to provide for them and their children. Whatever the source of their message, the forgiveness they ask for was already theirs.

questions: Seventeen years after Joseph forgave them, the brothers still feared his revenge. Why can it be so hard to believe we are forgiven, and what helps that belief take hold?
Joseph asks, “Am I in the place of God?” How does leaving judgment to God free a person to forgive without pretending the wrong did not happen?
Genesis ends with a coffin in Egypt and a promise not yet kept. What does it look like to live, and to die, holding on to a promise that has not yet been fulfilled?
